cards.explanation: The answer is anger. The writer opens with “How the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His anger!” From the very first line, this poem isn't tiptoeing in. You know right away what the weather is.

The answer is “Without pity.” The verse begins, “Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob.” The writer puts it right at the front, so you can't miss it. This is a poem of grief, and the writer says the loss plainly.

The answer is False, and the catch is in the second half. The writer says the Lord has “…withdrawn His right hand at the approach of the enemy.” So He holds back His hand instead of holding it out for Israel. The first half, cutting off every horn of Israel, is exactly what the verse says.

The answer is that He has bent His bow. The writer says, “He has bent His bow like an enemy; His right hand is positioned.” That's a picture of someone aimed and ready. The poem uses “…like an enemy…” to describe the scene, so I'll leave it right there.

The answer is True. The Lord has swallowed up Israel and all her palaces, and destroyed her strongholds. Then the writer says He “…has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah.” This is the verse where the grief piles up. I think the writer wants you to feel the weight of it.

The answer is her appointed feasts and Sabbaths. The writer says, “The LORD has made Zion forget her appointed feasts and Sabbaths.” Those were the special days that set the rhythm of her year. In the same verse, the Lord despises both king and priest.

The answer is False. The writer says the Lord, in His fierce anger, “…has despised both king and priest.” The priest is named right alongside the king, so “spared the priest” doesn't match the verse. That little word “both” is what settles this card.

The answer is in the house of the LORD. The writer says, “They have raised a shout in the house of the LORD as on the day of an appointed feast.” The enemy is shouting right inside the house of the LORD. I think that's why this line stings so much.

The answer is True. The gates have sunk into the ground, the king and princes are exiled among the nations, and the writer says “…the law is no more…” That's a lot of things going missing in one verse. Even the prophets are mentioned right after.
The answer is no vision. The writer says, “…even her prophets find no vision from the LORD.” Even her prophets, he says. The poem puts it plainly.

The answer is faint. The writer says his heart is poured out in grief because “…children and infants faint in the streets of the city.” This is the heart of why he's weeping. I think this is where the poem gets personal.

The answer is “Where is the grain and wine?” The children cry out to their mothers with those words. The writer says it as they faint like the wounded in the streets. I think this verse hurts, and it's okay to feel that.
The answer is False. The writer says, “…your wound is as deep as the sea. Who can ever heal you?” Nothing about it is small. He's looking for a way to console her, and even he can't find the words.

The answer is that they were empty and deceptive. The writer says, “The visions of your prophets were empty and deceptive…” He also says the burdens they envisioned were “…empty and misleading.” Those are the writer's own words for them.

The answer is False. The writer says her prophets “…did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity.” They didn't expose her guilt, and the captivity wasn't warded off. It's one of the sharpest lines in the poem.

The answer is that they clap their hands at her in scorn. The writer says, “All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn.” They hiss and shake their heads, too. It's a lot of noise for a city in ruins, and none of it is kind.

The answer is that they have waited for it. They say, “This is the day for which we have waited. We have lived to see it!” So they say they've waited for this day, and they're gloating now that it's here. That's a hard thing to hear from enemies.

The answer is True. The writer says, “The LORD has done what He planned; He has accomplished His decree, which He ordained in days of old…” So the decree goes back to days of old. The poem says it plainly and doesn't add why.

The answer is day and night. The poem says to let your tears run down like a river “…day and night.” Then it adds, “Give yourself no relief, and your eyes no rest.” It's a call to keep crying out, not to hold it in.

The answer is children. The poem says to lift up your hands to Him “…for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street.” That's who the prayer is for. I think it's a prayer you can feel.

The answer is “Whom have You ever treated like this?” The prayer says, “Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?” It's the poem speaking straight to the LORD. It asks Him to look first, and then it asks.

The answer is True. The prayer asks, “Should women eat their offspring, the infants they have nurtured?” Then it asks, “Should priests and prophets be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?” These are two very heavy questions. I think the poem is laying them before God on purpose.

The answer is False. The writer says, “In the day of the LORD’s anger no one escaped or survived…” So it isn't a few who made it out. The first part is true, since terrors were summoned on every side.
